transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I’m here because I’m not handling things right since my daughter left for basic training. I thought I’d be proud and keep busy, you know, work, the boat, my sculpture stuff—I used to make these metal pieces out of scrap, funny little fish and birds and things—but now I come home and the house just feels dead.

I’ve been crying in my truck before shifts, which is embarrassing because I work with a bunch of guys and you can’t exactly walk in with your face all blotchy. And at work I’m missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years. I snapped at one of the younger guys last week over something stupid. I just… I can’t keep myself together, and I don’t even want to go out on the water anymore. I don’t see the point.
How long have you been feeling this way since your daughter left for basic training?

About a month, I think. Since the day she left, really. I keep thinking it’ll settle down, like when she went away for summer camp once—though that was only a week and she was still little, with that ridiculous purple backpack—but this is different. So, yeah… it’s been about a month of feeling like this.
Are you still enjoying your sculpture work or has that changed for you too?

Yeah… that’s changed too. I used to go out back and mess with scrap metal for hours—little birds, fish, whatever came into my head. I had this one piece I was making out of an old fender, and it was going to be kind of funny-looking, like one of those herons that hangs around the marina… 

But since my daughter left, I just come home and the house feels dead. I look at the tools and the metal and I just… don’t see the point. Same with going out on the water. I’m barely keeping it together before work, crying in my truck and then trying not to mess up jobs I’ve done forever, and then I snap at the younger guys over nothing. So no, I’m not really enjoying it. I’ve pretty much stopped.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

Not really… I try to think of something, but everything I used to look forward to just feels flat. I used to love taking the boat out, even if it was just to sit there with coffee and complain about the gulls stealing bait—there was this one spot I’d go where the water got real still in the morning…

But now since my daughter left for basic training, I come home and it’s like the house is dead. I don’t go out on the water, I don’t mess with my scrap metal sculptures. I look at it all and just think, what’s the point? I’m mostly just trying to get through work without crying in the truck first or messing up welding steps I’ve done for years. I even snap at the younger guys sometimes, and that’s not me. So… no, I can’t say there’s anything I’m really looking forward to right now.
Do you feel guilty about anything related to your daughter leaving for basic training?

I don’t know… guilty? I mean, I keep turning that word over and I’m not sure if that’s what it is. I’m proud of her, you know—she’s always been stubborn, even when she was little and insisted on tying her own shoes wrong for half a year.

But guilt… I guess I don’t know exactly. I keep thinking about little things I could’ve said different, but then I don’t know if that’s guilt or just me missing her and my head running around in circles. What do you mean by guilty, exactly?
Do you feel like you've done something wrong or made a mistake related to your daughter leaving for basic training?

I don’t… I don’t think I did something wrong exactly. She chose it, you know? She’s the one who went and talked to the recruiter and got all fired up about it.

I keep replaying stupid little things, like whether I should’ve asked more questions or maybe acted more excited instead of getting quiet. And then I think about when she was a kid and wanted to climb everything—fence posts, the old workbench, even that half-busted picnic table we had—and I’d be yelling, “Get down before you break your neck,” and she’d just grin at me like I was the unreasonable one.

So… made a mistake? I don’t know. Maybe not. I’m just stuck wondering if I handled it right, I guess.
Are there any small things that you still find pleasure in, even if it's just for a moment?

Maybe for a second here and there… like, I’ll get a cup of coffee and it’s hot enough and tastes right, and I think, okay, that’s something. But it doesn’t last.

Mostly I come home and the place just feels dead since she left. I’ll stand there with my keys still in my hand like I forgot what I’m supposed to do next. I used to go out on the water or mess with those scrap metal pieces—made a heron once out of old brackets and sheet scraps, looked ridiculous until I got the neck right—but now I look at the boat or the metal pile and I just… I don’t see the point.

Even at work I’m not keeping myself together. Crying in the truck before a shift, missing welding steps I could do half-asleep, snapping at the younger guys when they’re just asking normal questions. So small things? I guess maybe a sip of coffee, maybe the dog next door doing something dumb, but it goes flat pretty quick.
Do you feel sad most of the day?

Yeah… most of the day, I think so. It’s like it’s waiting for me when I get home. Since she left for basic training, the house just feels… dead. Too quiet.

I’ll be okay for a bit at work maybe, or I’ll think I’m okay, and then I’m sitting in my truck before a shift crying like an idiot, trying to pull myself together before anybody sees. And then I still mess up—missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years. Snapping at the younger guys when they’re just asking me something normal.

I used to go out on the water when my head got loud, or mess around with scrap metal, make something out of nothing. I had this piece I was working on, sort of a bird shape, and now I just look at it and think… why bother. So yeah. Sad’s probably the word. Most of the day, yeah.
Are there any activities that you still enjoy or find pleasurable, even if it's just a little bit?

Not really. I mean, I used to like taking the boat out, just getting on the water where everything kind of spreads out and gets quieter. And I used to mess around with scrap metal after work—little sculpture things, nothing fancy. I had one I was working on and now it’s just sitting there.

Since my daughter left for basic training, I come home and the house feels dead. I’ll look at the boat or the metal and just think… what’s the point. Even work’s been off—I’m crying in the truck before shifts, missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years, snapping at the younger guys when they’re only asking normal stuff.

So, activities I enjoy… no, not much. Maybe for a minute, but it doesn’t stay.
Are there any activities that you find yourself looking forward to at all?

Looking forward to? Not really… I keep thinking maybe I should take the boat out, because that used to help, you know, just being on the water. But then I get home and the house feels dead since my daughter left for basic training, and I just kind of stop in the doorway.

I’ve got this sculpture sitting there too, scrap metal pieces all over, and normally I’d tinker with that for hours. Now I look at it and I just don’t see the point. Same with work—I’m not even holding it together there, crying in the truck before shifts, missing welding steps I’ve done forever, snapping at the younger guys. So no… I can’t say there’s much I’m actually looking forward to.
Are there any activities that give you pleasure?

Pleasure… no, not really. I mean, the boat used to. I’d go out on the water and it’d settle me down some. And I had that scrap metal sculpture I was working on—my daughter used to say it looked like a weird bird, which… she wasn’t wrong.

But since she left for basic training, I come home and it’s just this dead house, you know? Too quiet. I’ll see the boat, or that half-finished thing sitting there, and I just… I don’t see the point.

Even before work, I’m sitting in my truck crying, trying to get myself together, and then I’m still messing up welding steps I’ve done for years. Snapping at the younger guys too, and they’re not even doing anything wrong. So… no. I can’t really say anything’s giving me pleasure right now.
Do you feel anxious most of the day?

I don’t know if I’d call it anxious most of the day. I mean, I get wound up, sure, but “most of the day” is hard to say. Sometimes it’s just like I’m standing there thinking about one thing and then I’m thinking about ten other things, like whether I locked the shed or if I left tools out, and then I realize I’m not even answering what you asked.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really been tracking it like that.
Do you feel anxious?

I mean… anxious like nervous? I don’t know. Sometimes I get keyed up, but then sometimes I’m just sort of blank, and I don’t know what you’d call that.

Like yesterday I stood in the kitchen trying to remember why I’d opened the drawer, and then I noticed this old takeout menu stuck to the fridge from that Thai place that closed, which is stupid because I don’t even know why I kept it—sorry, that’s not what you asked.

I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t really thought of it as “anxious” exactly.
Do you feel anxious?

I’m sorry, I know you asked that already. I guess I’m having trouble pinning it down. Like, my body feels worked up sometimes, but then I start thinking about whether I paid the electric bill or why the neighbor’s dog keeps barking at the same time every night, and then I’m off somewhere else in my head.

So… do I feel anxious? Maybe sometimes? I don’t know if that’s the right word for it.
Do you feel anxious?

I keep getting stuck on the word, I guess. Like if you mean do I feel scared or panicky, I don’t know that I’d say it that way. Sometimes I’m just… wound tight.

But then I start trying to explain it and I’m thinking about work gloves I lost last week, and whether I left them in the truck or at the shop, and then I realize I still didn’t answer you straight. So… I’m not sure. I notice I’m tense sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s “anxious.”
Do you feel anxious?

I don’t know how to answer it better than… I can’t really tell. Like, if I say yes, that sounds too definite, and if I say no, that doesn’t feel right either.

I notice I get all caught up trying to figure out what I’m supposed to be feeling, and then I’m thinking about the clock on the wall ticking too loud, or whether I parked in the right spot outside, and then I lose the thread.

So… maybe? But I’m not sure I’d call it anxious.
Do you feel anxious?

I’m sorry, I feel like I’m going in circles with this. I don’t know. I notice I’m… keyed up sometimes, but then I start wondering if that’s anxiety or just being tired, or if I drank too much coffee, and then I’m thinking about the break room coffee at work and how it tastes burnt every single day.

So I guess I can’t give you a clean yes or no. I haven’t really sorted out if what I’m feeling is anxiety.
Do you feel nervous?

Nervous… I don’t know. That’s kind of like anxious, right? Or maybe it’s different, like when you’re waiting for someone to yell your name and you don’t know if you’re in trouble.

I mean, I get this sort of tight feeling sometimes, but then I start thinking maybe everybody gets that, especially when there’s too much going on. Like at work, there’s always noise, metal banging, somebody needing something, and then I’m thinking about whether I put my tools back in the right place, and—

Sorry. I don’t really know if I’d call it nervous. I’m not sure.
Have you had any thoughts about death or wanting to die since your daughter left for basic training?

I… I don’t know. That feels like a big question, and when you say it that way I kind of freeze up.

Since she left, I’ve had a lot of thoughts that kind of spin around, but I don’t know if I’d put that in the category of wanting to die. Sometimes I’ll be driving and miss a turn because I’m thinking about whether she’s eating enough, which is stupid because they feed them there, obviously, but then I think about the boots and if they gave her the right size because she always hated stiff shoes when she was little—

Sorry. I’m not trying to avoid it. I just… I don’t think I know how to answer that clearly.
Have you had any thoughts about wanting to die or harming yourself since your daughter left for basic training?

I… I’m not sure. When you say “harming myself,” I start thinking about, like, what counts as that, and then my head goes off somewhere else. I don’t think I’ve sat down and thought it through that way.

Since she left, I’ve just been… I don’t know, my brain gets stuck on her being gone, and then I’ll remember her packing socks, and whether I should’ve bought her better ones, and then I’m standing there holding laundry detergent like an idiot because I forgot why I went into the room.

So… I don’t really have a clear answer. I’m not trying to be difficult. I just don’t know how to put it.
